narration: A missing part may be a few dozen pixels. Inspection asks: does what the camera sees match what should be there?

narration: LoopCheck is a research prototype for agentic visual inspection. Rather than one opaque label, it returns a decision and its evidence.
visual_cue: Wordmark reveal; reference vs inspection; divider wipe over the registered (aligned) inspection; statement: decision + rule + tool trace.

narration: Its agent is a rule-based controller, not a neural network. It calls OpenCV tools in turn: register the images, then compare them into an anomaly map. Extra checks run only when the evidence calls for them.
visual_cue: Flow: inputs -> controller -> R0 register -> R1 compare -> evidence + decision. Real homography warp, real heatmap and candidate (peak 0.94, 1831 px), C0 confirm, T1 DEFECT; conditional tools strip.

narration: Here is the running app. An unchanged tray is approved. A missing component is a confirmed defect. A faint, tiny object can't be confirmed, so the agent escalates to human review instead of guessing.
visual_cue: Real Streamlit screenshots (local mode): Clean -> APPROVE T5; Missing part -> DEFECT T1 with overlay close-up; Ambiguous tiny object -> HUMAN_REVIEW T2 with the agent trace.

narration: Strong evidence is confirmed directly; weaker regions must be reproduced by independent views, or go to a person. The same controller runs on AWS Lambda behind API Gateway, returning the decision, its rule and the tool trace.

narration: On a held-out synthetic test set, it made no automatic errors and sent about a third of cases to review. That's synthetic validation, not real-world performance, and the scores aren't probabilities.
